"All my life, its been Hitler this and Hitler that. Finally, I took it upon myself to read Hitler's magnum opus, Mein Kampf."

Hitler had a biocentric worldview. His perspective on life was first of all referenced in Nature. Hitler contended that before anything else we must attend to Nature, the world of living things and their environments. Man is not separate from or above Nature but rather a part of Nature. We need to come to grips with how Nature actually operates. We must align our lives with Nature. We must obey Nature’s laws. That is how we will best prosper and fulfill our destiny as human beings.

Very interesting.

I suppose I shouldn't be surprised how reminiscent these ideas are of the alt right. There are solid axioms: outcome is a product of nature and nurture; people are not universally equal; nature, to be commanded, must first be obeyed; mixing good with bad does not make better.

But the critical flaw is collectivism. He goes too far in generalizing races. He focuses on the group over the individual, rather than allowing for merits and ability to be judged on an individual level, and allowing people to make decisions accordingly. He has mistaken beliefs about the effectiveness of a society based on heirarchy and control. In reality, progress is made by competition and survival from chaos, not tight control. Central planning of anything, from economics to genetics, is at best fragile, and at worst, catastrophic.

Finally, while there is reason to be sceptical of democracy, his alternative of "ruler of personality" is a poor solution. First of all, the primary benefit of democracy is credibility, because it gets buy-in from the electorate (no matter how superficial), so that society respects the authority they are governed by. Secondly, his idea of leaders being determined by "survival of the fittest" is absolutely just as vulnerable to a "bad but charismatic leader" as democracy.

His conclusions about eugenics and education and such seem to follow logically from the preceding premises. It's his belief in collectivism that is the flaw. It's really no wonder that he led the "National Socialist" party. He believed that you could make a good society by getting everyone to be subservient to the collective. This is nonsense that was roundly disproven time and again in the 20th century.

This is how it reminds me of the alt right. I've long viewed the alt right as people with good basic values (concerning culture and what is good in society) who have been corrupted by the exit and mistaken leftist idea of collectivism (whereby accomplishments and sins are shared by the entire race, and group identity supercedes individual merit). The alt right seems to shy away from the authoritarian implications of collectivism (unlike Hitler), but the identitarian mistakes are the same.

It's fascinating to me, because I've viewed the alt right as conservatives who have been poisoned by the identity politics of the modern left. But seeing the same pattern in Hitler's basic worldview makes me want to learn more about it's origins.
